opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, in a startup, the hardest part isn't finding things to do. It's deciding what *not* to do. There are always a hundred things that look important, and as a small team you can maybe do three of them well.

So the way I think about it is in a few layers. First, what keeps the company alive? That means customers and the product they actually pay for. If a customer is blocked, that comes before almost anything else, because trust is very hard to win back. Second, what moves us toward where we want to be in six months or a year? That's usually the technical bets and the product direction, and it's easy to neglect because it never feels urgent today. I try to protect some time for it every week, otherwise the urgent stuff eats everything.

Third, and people underestimate this one, is the team. When you're small, every hire changes the culture. So recruiting and making sure people have what they need isn't a side task. It's core work for me as a founder.

I also coming from a big company background have had to unlearn some habits. At a large company you can afford to build things very thoroughly, with lots of process. In a startup you have to accept that some things will be good enough for now, ship it, learn from users, and iterate. The trick is knowing which parts can be rough and which parts, like reliability or security, absolutely cannot.

And lastly, I try to stay close to the actual work: talking to users, looking at the code, trying the product myself. If you only look at dashboards and meetings, you lose your sense of what really matters, and then your priorities drift without you noticing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the way I think about priorities has changed a lot since I left big companies and started Lepton. At Meta or Alibaba, you could afford to think in terms of roadmaps and quarters. In a startup, the first thing you learn is that the roadmap is a hypothesis, and reality corrects it every week.

So the first filter I apply is very simple: does this thing directly help a customer get value out of our product today, or does it make it meaningfully easier for the next customer to do so? If the answer is no, it goes to the bottom of the list, no matter how intellectually interesting it is. That's a hard discipline for someone with a research background. I built Caffe because it was fun and because I wanted to understand things. In a startup, "fun" and "I want to understand this" can't be the primary reason to spend engineering time. They can be a happy side effect.

The second filter is about leverage. We're a small team, and the AI infrastructure space moves absurdly fast. New models come out every week, hardware availability shifts, and prices change. So I ask myself: where are the few decisions that, if we get them right, make a lot of downstream problems disappear? For us that's things like how we abstract the underlying GPU resources, how we make deployment reproducible, and how we keep the developer experience simple even when the stack underneath is messy. If we invest in those well, we don't have to firefight the same issue a hundred times.

And then the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is protecting the team's time. Priorities aren't just a list of what to do. They're also a list of what to say no to. A startup dies not from one big mistake but from a hundred small distractions that each seemed reasonable. Someone asks for a feature, a partner wants a custom integration, a conference invites you to speak. Every one of those is defensible in isolation. Collectively they kill your focus. So part of my job as a founder is to be the person who says, "That's a good idea, and we're not doing it right now."

Practically, on a daily basis, this means I spend my mornings on whatever is blocking customers or blocking engineers, because unblocking people compounds. I try to reserve some uninterrupted time for the one or two things that only I can do, usually around technical direction or key relationships. And I try to end the day by asking whether the things we did today actually moved us toward being useful to people, or whether we just stayed busy. Those two feel identical in the moment and are completely different in hindsight.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is deciding what not to do. In a startup, there are always more things you could work on than you have people or time for. So I try to ask: What is the most important uncertainty we need to resolve right now? Is it whether customers actually need the product, whether the technology works, or whether we can deliver it reliably?

That helps me prioritize day to day. If a customer is blocked, I want to understand why. Sometimes it’s a technical problem, but sometimes we’ve misunderstood how they want to use the product. You have to stay close enough to the customer to tell the difference.

And as a founder, I have to keep asking whether something really needs my attention or whether I should give someone else the context and ownership to handle it. Otherwise, my own time becomes the bottleneck. The priorities change, but the goal is to keep the team focused on the few things that move the company forward.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes understanding customer needs and prioritizing product uncertainties, but it does not compare this with personally writing code or say it takes priority over coding.

r002.rationale: The response says to delegate ownership so the founder does not become a bottleneck, but it does not describe using remaining time for work teammates lack time to handle.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most important thing is figuring out which problems actually matter right now. In a startup, there are always more things you could do than you have people or time to do them. So I try to start with the customer: What are they trying to accomplish? Where are they getting stuck? And what can we do that would make a meaningful difference?

Then you have to be very disciplined about focus. As an engineer, it’s tempting to work on an interesting technical problem, but the most interesting problem isn’t necessarily the most important one for the company. Sometimes the priority is improving the product; sometimes it’s hiring the right person or helping the team make a decision.

I think of priorities as something you keep revisiting. You need a clear direction, but you also need to be willing to change your plan when you learn something new.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes starting with customer needs and says an interesting technical problem may not be the company’s most important priority. It does not clearly say Yangqing Jia prioritizes aligning customer needs with system development over personally writing code.
